title: From light to ATP and NADPH

scenes.visual: A photon lifts an electron; if not captured it relaxes as heat or fluorescence; at the reaction center the electron moves to an acceptor (charge separation).
scenes.narration: Trace the fate of a single photon in three panels. First, absorption. Only a photon with the right energy can promote an electron in the pigment from the ground state to an excited state. Second, what happens if that energy is not captured quickly enough? The excited electron simply relaxes, releasing the energy as heat or fluorescence, and the opportunity is lost. Third, the productive route at the reaction center. The excited pigment hands its electron to a primary acceptor, creating charge separation. That moment, where an electron physically moves rather than the energy merely transferring, is where photosynthesis truly begins.

scenes.visual: Antenna pigments pass energy by resonance (electrons stay put); a funnel feeds one reaction center where an electron physically moves.
scenes.narration: Light harvesting and chemistry are two distinct jobs, and this funnel shows the handoff. On the left, in the antenna system, two to three hundred pigments pass excitation energy from donor to acceptor by resonance transfer. The energy hops, but the electrons themselves stay put, and efficiency falls off steeply with distance. All of that captured energy is funneled into a single reaction center on the right. There the special pair, P680 or P700, finally does something different. It gives up an actual electron to an acceptor. Energy transfer concentrates the harvest. Electron transfer in the reaction center commits it to chemistry.

scenes.visual: Thylakoid membrane circuit: water split at PSII, lumen protons, PSI, NADPH on stroma side, ATP synthase.
scenes.narration: Here is the whole light reaction circuit drawn across the thylakoid membrane. Start at the left. Water is split at photosystem II, releasing oxygen and protons and feeding electrons into the chain. Light excites P680, then P700 at photosystem I, lifting electrons twice. As electrons flow, protons accumulate inside the thylakoid lumen, building a concentration gradient. NADP plus is reduced to NADPH on the stromal side. Finally, that proton gradient drives ATP synthase, which makes ATP. In one picture, light in at two photosystems, water split, protons pumped, and the two energy currencies, NADPH and ATP, produced together.

As electrons flow, protons accumulate inside the thylakoid lumen, building a concentration gradient. NADP-plus is reduced to NADPH on the stromal side. Finally, that proton gradient drives ATP synthase, which makes ATP. In one picture: light in at two photosystems, water split, protons pumped, and the two energy currencies, NADPH and ATP, produced together.

scenes.visual: Energy diagram: two light-driven uphill jumps with a downhill slide between that pumps protons; ATP and NADPH.
scenes.narration: The two photosystems work as partners in a choreographed two-step. Photosystem II leads. It splits water molecules and releases the oxygen we breathe, and its electrons drop in energy to build a proton gradient that powers ATP synthesis. Photosystem I follows. A second hit of light re-energizes the electrons so they can produce NADPH, the reducing power that ultimately enables sugar production. Read the energy diagram as two uphill jumps powered by light, with a downhill slide between them that pumps protons. Two light-driven boosts, one to make ATP, one to make NADPH.

scenes.visual: PSII tally: 4 photons + 2 H2O in; 4 e- on QH2, 4 H+ in the lumen, O2 out.
scenes.narration: Let us tally exactly what Photosystem II does in one balanced statement. Inputs on the left: four photons of light and two molecules of water. The machine in the middle, with its P680 reaction center, splits that water. The outputs on the right are remarkable. Electrons leave on plastoquinol, the QH2 carrier, headed for cytochrome b6f. Four protons are deposited in the lumen, feeding the gradient. And oxygen gas is released, arguably the most important waste product in history. One machine, four photons, two waters, and the breathable atmosphere is a byproduct of charging the electron transport chain.
